electrical_safety.name: electrical_safety
electrical_safety.description: Electrical safety refers to the identification, prevention, and control of hazards related to the use of electrical systems and equipment in the workplace. It encompasses safe work practices, proper equipment maintenance, and hazard recognition to prevent electrical injuries, shocks, burns, or fires. Observations in this category often involve unsafe wiring, improper use of electrical tools, or lack of protective measures.
examples: Observed missing covers on electrical panels in the maintenance room.
Extension cords found running across walkways without protection.
Worker using damaged power tool with exposed wires.
No lockout/tagout applied during electrical maintenance.
Unlabeled circuit breakers in the main distribution board.

arc_flash.name: arc_flash
arc_flash.description: Arc flash refers to a dangerous electrical explosion caused by a rapid release of energy due to an electrical arc, often resulting in severe burns, injuries, or equipment damage. In HSE, this category covers incidents, near misses, or hazards where workers are exposed to arc flash risks, typically during maintenance or operation of high-voltage equipment. Observations may include inadequate PPE, improper procedures, or lack of arc flash labeling.
examples: Worker entered switchgear room without arc flash PPE.
Arc flash warning label missing on main panel.
Observed burn marks near circuit breaker after arc event.
Maintenance performed on live equipment without arc flash analysis.
Near miss: arc flash occurred during breaker racking.

fire_risk.name: fire_risk
fire_risk.description: Fire risk involves the potential for ignition, spread, and consequences of fire in the workplace, often due to electrical faults, flammable materials, or equipment malfunction. In HSE, this category includes observations of conditions or behaviors that could lead to fire incidents, such as overloaded circuits, blocked fire exits, or improper storage of combustibles. It is critical for preventing property damage, injuries, and fatalities.
examples: Overloaded power strip found under desk with multiple devices.
Flammable liquids stored near electrical panels.
Fire extinguisher blocked by storage boxes.
Accumulation of dust on electrical equipment increasing fire risk.
Observed sparks from faulty outlet in production area.

short_circuit.name: short_circuit
short_circuit.description: Short circuit refers to an abnormal connection between two points in an electrical circuit, causing excessive current flow and potential overheating, equipment damage, or fire. In HSE, this category covers incidents, hazards, or near misses involving short circuits, often due to faulty wiring, damaged insulation, or improper repairs. Observations may include tripped breakers, burnt smells, or visible arcing.
examples: Breaker tripped due to short circuit in lighting circuit.
Burnt smell detected near control panel after shorting event.
Observed sparks from exposed wires causing a short.
Short circuit caused emergency shutdown of conveyor system.
Technician reported melted insulation from shorted cable.

wiring_fault.name: wiring_fault
wiring_fault.description: Wiring fault refers to defects or failures in electrical wiring, such as loose connections, damaged insulation, or incorrect installations, which can lead to electrical hazards. In HSE, this category includes observations of unsafe or non-compliant wiring that could cause shocks, fires, or equipment malfunctions. Typical events involve exposed conductors, improper terminations, or signs of overheating.
examples: Loose wire connections found in junction box.
Damaged insulation on power cable in workshop.
Improperly terminated wires in control cabinet.
Observed overheating at wire connection point.
Exposed conductor found during routine inspection.

equipment_failure.name: equipment_failure
equipment_failure.description: Equipment failure refers to the malfunction or breakdown of electrical or mechanical devices, which can create safety hazards, disrupt operations, or lead to incidents. In HSE, this category includes observations where equipment does not operate as intended, potentially exposing workers to risks such as shock, fire, or mechanical injury. Examples include failed circuit breakers, non-functioning alarms, or defective tools.
examples: Main circuit breaker failed to trip during overload.
Emergency stop button not functioning on conveyor.
Observed smoke from failed motor in pump room.
Alarm system did not activate during test.
Power tool stopped working due to internal fault.

overload.name: overload
overload.description: Overload refers to a condition where electrical circuits or equipment are subjected to currents or loads exceeding their rated capacity, increasing the risk of overheating, fire, or equipment damage. In HSE, this category covers observations of overloaded outlets, panels, or machinery, often due to improper use or lack of load management. It is a common cause of electrical incidents and fire hazards.
examples: Multiple high-power devices plugged into single outlet.
Observed tripped breaker due to circuit overload.
Extension cord used beyond rated capacity.
Panel board showing signs of overheating from overload.
Machinery shut down after exceeding load limit.

ground_fault.name: ground_fault
ground_fault.description: Ground fault refers to an unintentional electrical path between a power source and the ground, which can result in electric shock, equipment damage, or fire. In HSE, this category includes incidents or hazards where current leaks to ground due to insulation failure, damaged wiring, or faulty equipment. Observations may involve tripped ground fault interrupters, tingling sensations, or visible arcing.
examples: GFCI outlet tripped during equipment operation.
Worker reported tingling sensation when touching metal enclosure.
Detected ground fault in lighting circuit during inspection.
Observed arcing at grounding connection.
Ground fault alarm activated in control room.

exposed_wiring.name: exposed_wiring
exposed_wiring.description: Exposed wiring refers to electrical conductors that are not properly insulated or covered, posing a risk of electric shock, burns, or fire. In HSE, this category includes observations of wires left uncovered, damaged insulation, or temporary wiring setups that do not meet safety standards. Such conditions are often found during maintenance, renovations, or after equipment damage.
examples: Exposed wires found hanging from ceiling in storage area.
Damaged insulation on extension cord near workbench.
Temporary wiring left uncovered after repair work.
Observed bare conductors in electrical panel.
Loose wires present near water source.

power_outage.name: power_outage
power_outage.description: Power outage refers to the loss of electrical power supply to a facility, area, or equipment, which can disrupt operations and create safety hazards. In HSE, this category includes incidents or observations where power loss affects critical systems, emergency lighting, or safe evacuation. Causes may include equipment failure, grid issues, or planned maintenance.
examples: Unexpected power outage halted production line.
Emergency lighting failed to activate during blackout.
Power loss affected ventilation system in confined space.
Planned power shutdown for maintenance announced.
Critical alarms did not function during power interruption.

shock_hazard.name: shock_hazard
shock_hazard.description: Shock hazard refers to the risk of electric shock to personnel due to contact with live electrical parts, faulty equipment, or improper grounding. In HSE, this category includes observations of unsafe conditions where workers could be exposed to electrical currents, such as exposed wiring, wet environments, or lack of protective devices. Preventing shock hazards is essential for worker safety.
examples: Worker received mild shock from metal tool near live panel.
Wet floor observed around electrical outlet.
No insulating mat provided at switchboard.
Exposed live wires found in maintenance area.
Improperly grounded equipment posing shock risk.
